units.title: Form 4 VA Intro: Course and SBA Portfolio
units.intro: Form 4 starter unit. Learn the two learning strands (appreciation and making), positive values, and the basic SBA portfolio structure (research workbook + artwork/critical studies). Aligned to CCCKLC F.4 Syllabus 25–26 Orientation and SBA criteria notes. No real HKEAA papers or high-score student exemplars. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: Two Strands: Appreciation and Making
cards: Form 4 Visual Arts follows the official curriculum with two main strands: visual arts appreciation and visual arts making.
Appreciation: learn to look at artworks, understand signs and styles, and the historical, social and cultural contexts of art.
Making: learn to use materials and techniques to express ideas, turning experience and feeling into visual form.
Throughout both strands, build an open and respectful attitude toward different cultures and viewpoints.
[No cleared image yet] Later: a simple two-strand diagram (self-made / CC0).

quiz.question: What are the two main learning strands in the VA curriculum?
quiz.explain: The curriculum emphasises visual arts appreciation and visual arts making.

quiz.question: Appreciation often includes describe, analyse, interpret and ____ artworks.
quiz.explain: A common four-step critical frame is describe–analyse–interpret–judge (Feldman-aligned).

quiz.question: What does the making strand emphasise?
options: Using media and skills to express your own ideas
quiz.answer: Using media and skills to express your own ideas
quiz.explain: Making turns ideas and experience into visual form while building skill.

quiz.question: Match each focus
quiz.explain: All three work together in VA learning.

lessons.title: SBA Portfolio: Research Workbook and Artwork/Critical Studies
cards: School-based Assessment (SBA) usually means one portfolio: a research workbook plus artwork/critical studies.
Artwork/critical studies: about four pieces under one theme; some may be written critical studies (follow school and official guidance).
The research workbook shows theme exploration, study of related artworks, media experiments and reflection on progress.
Assessment focuses on media skills, visual presentation, relationship with context, creativity/imagination, overall theme communication and progression.
This lesson covers structure only. It does not provide real HKEAA papers or high-score student exemplars.

quiz.question: An SBA portfolio usually includes which two parts?
quiz.explain: Official SBA centres on the research workbook plus artwork/critical studies.

quiz.question: The research workbook develops a theme that the student ____.
quiz.explain: The theme is self-selected and developed over time.

quiz.question: Which item should NOT appear in this platform's demo content?
quiz.explain: VA-Nexus does not reproduce real HKEAA papers or high-score student exemplars.

quiz.question: Match portfolio parts to roles

answer.Artwork/critical studies: Visual works or critical writing under the theme

quiz.explain: The two parts work together to show process and outcomes.

units.title: Drawing, Aesthetics and Design Thinking
units.intro: Aligned to F.4 Scheme “Creative Practice 2”: drawing skills, aesthetic/design thinking, material exploration and presentation skills. Builds observation, composition and material foundations for later theme work. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: Observation and Drawing Basics: Line, Shape, Composition
cards: Drawing from observation starts with looking: overall shape and proportion first, details later—not deepest shadows first.
Basic visual elements: line, shape, colour, texture, space. Organising principles: contrast, rhythm, balance, emphasis.
Try compositions such as rule of thirds, diagonal guides and empty space. Different compositions change where viewers look first.
Wucius Wong brought design principles into ink landscape, showing how structure can organise a picture.
[No cleared image yet] Later: self-made line/shape drills, or an official museum page about Wucius Wong (text + link).

quiz.question: A better way to start observational drawing is to:
options: Observe overall shape and proportion first
Ignore the subject and invent everything
quiz.answer: Observe overall shape and proportion first
quiz.explain: Stable overall proportions make details easier.

quiz.question: Visual elements include line, shape, colour, texture and ____.
quiz.explain: Space (depth, layers, empty areas) is a key element.

quiz.question: Wucius Wong’s practice reminds us that:
options: Design structure can organise a picture
quiz.answer: Design structure can organise a picture
quiz.explain: He reorganised ink landscapes with geometric/design-based composition.

quiz.question: Match element/principle

answer.Emphasis: Guides viewers to look somewhere first

quiz.explain: Organising principles control how people look.

lessons.title: Aesthetics, Design Thinking and Material Exploration
cards: Aesthetic/design thinking: define a problem → generate options → prototype → test/reflect → improve.
Material exploration: try the same theme in pencil, charcoal, ink, collage, etc., and note which medium best serves your intention.
Presentation skills: state your theme, why you chose the medium, and how composition and symbols carry meaning.
Practice: pick one everyday object; make it twice in two media; write three sentences comparing which fits your theme better.
[No cleared image yet] Later: a self-made material-experiment comparison chart.

quiz.question: Design thinking is closest to which flow?
options: Submit a final once with no reflection
quiz.explain: Design thinking is iterative and reflective.

quiz.question: In material exploration, record which medium best expresses your ____.
quiz.explain: Medium choices should serve creative intention.

quiz.question: In a presentation you should at least cover:
options: Theme, reasons for medium, and how composition/symbols communicate
quiz.answer: Theme, reasons for medium, and how composition/symbols communicate
quiz.explain: Link ideas to visual decisions.

units.title: Community Looking, Visual Diary and Theme Seeds
units.intro: Aligned to F.4 community tour/presentation, weekly visual diary, and community-related design/making. Learn to gather materials from everyday environments as theme seeds; connect to Hong Kong artists who attend to daily space. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: Weekly Visual Diary: How to Observe and Record
cards: A visual diary is a year-long habit: each week record what you see and feel, plus small experiments, in images and short notes.
You can include quick compositions, colour notes, tiny material trials, and one “today I noticed…” line.
The point is not perfect pages but steady observation and reflection—later theme work will use these materials.
Tip: keep one small book or digital folder; date + place + one reflection sentence.
[No cleared image yet] Later: a blank visual-diary layout template (self-made).

quiz.question: What matters most in a visual diary?
options: Every page must be a finished masterpiece
quiz.explain: The diary is a process tool for later themes and the portfolio.

quiz.question: Each entry should note date, place and one ____.
quiz.explain: Reflection turns looking into usable ideas.

quiz.question: How can a visual diary be used later?
options: As material for theme development and the research workbook
Only torn up and never reused
quiz.answer: As material for theme development and the research workbook
quiz.explain: Diaries feed theme work and the RWB.

lessons.title: Community Tour: Finding a Theme in the Environment
cards: A community tour can use photos, short video, interviews, collected objects, sketches or actions to record the environment and learning.
Making can relate to community: public space, neighbourhood routines, local signs—then reconnect to your theme.
Pak Sheung Chuen often uses everyday actions and ready-mades to make housing/space experiences visible.
Lee Kit often uses household cloth and everyday objects to speak about private feeling and space—community and personal life can be read together.

Practice: walk a familiar street; collect three notes on symbol/object/sound; write how each could become a theme question. Contemporary works: [no cleared image] — text + official collection pages only.

quiz.question: Community-tour materials can include:
options: Photos, interviews, sketches, collected objects, etc.
Imagination with no leaving the classroom ever
quiz.answer: Photos, interviews, sketches, collected objects, etc.
quiz.explain: Diverse sources help theme exploration.

quiz.question: Pak Sheung Chuen’s practice often makes everyday ____ experience visible.
quiz.explain: For example, bagging a flat’s air to respond to cramped housing.

quiz.question: Match artist to focus

answer.Pak Sheung Chuen: Everyday actions / pressure of urban space
answer.Lee Kit: Household objects and private emotional space

quiz.explain: Both start from the everyday, with different focuses.

quiz.question: After gathering community materials, a good next step is to:
options: Ask a theme question you can keep exploring
Demand real exam papers from the platform
quiz.answer: Ask a theme question you can keep exploring
quiz.explain: A theme question drives research and making.

units.title: Self-Portrait, Artist Research and Theme Development
units.intro: Aligned to F.4 “Theme and Artist research and Presentation I (Self-Portrait)” and discovery prompts Self / Relationship / Story. Use self-portrait to explore identity and practise proper artist research (cite sources, compare views) to start SBA theme development. No high-score student exemplars. (Content pending teacher review)

lessons.title: Self-Portrait and Identity: Self, Relationship, Story
cards: A self-portrait is more than likeness: it can speak about identity, bodily experience, roles and social gaze.
School prompts can open three doors: Self (a collection of curiosities), Relationship (family objects), Story (conflict or tension).
Frida Kahlo used self-portrait to speak personal experience and cultural identity—the learning goal is how symbols tell a self, not copying a style for marks.
Wilson Shieh paints contemporary figures in gongbi to explore Hong Kong identity; David Hockney often paints family and looking—useful for a “relationship” theme.
Copyrighted/contemporary works: [no cleared image] — classroom text + museum/reliable encyclopedia sources; public-domain historic self-portraits can be added later.

quiz.question: A self-portrait can explore:
options: Identity, relationships, personal story and social gaze
quiz.answer: Identity, relationships, personal story and social gaze
quiz.explain: Self-portrait is a common entry to theme and identity research.

quiz.question: School theme doors include Self, Relationship and ____.
quiz.explain: Story can mean conflict, tension or a narrative line.

quiz.question: Match artist to entry point

answer.Wilson Shieh: Gongbi contemporary figures and HK identity

quiz.explain: All three can inspire self-portrait/relationship themes in different media and contexts.

quiz.question: When referencing artists, the right move is to:
options: Understand how they use symbols, then develop your own view
Copy a work exactly as your own
Only paste images with no thinking
quiz.answer: Understand how they use symbols, then develop your own view
quiz.explain: Research is for dialogue and inspiration, not cloning.

lessons.title: How to Do Artist Research and a Theme Presentation
cards: Artist-research steps: choose relevant artists → record basics → study form and context → link to your theme → write a personal view with evidence.
Use reliable sources: museums, galleries, textbooks, teacher notes; separate facts from opinions.
Presentation I suggested structure: theme question → self/relationship entry → 1–2 artist comparisons → next media experiments.
The research workbook should show process: drafts, experiments, failures and improvements—not only final pretty photos.
Reminder: no full real exam papers and no “high-score” student exemplars.

quiz.question: Artist research should end with:
options: A personal view with evidence, linked to your theme
quiz.answer: A personal view with evidence, linked to your theme
quiz.explain: Research must serve theme development.

quiz.question: A presentation should include theme question, entry point, artist comparison and next ____ experiments.
quiz.explain: Media experiments turn research into making.

quiz.question: A research workbook should show:
quiz.explain: Progression and reflection matter in SBA.

quiz.question: Match research steps

answer.Link to theme: State what it sparks for your making

quiz.explain: These steps stop research from becoming a dump of facts.
